post.instagram:
Send this to the parent who worries about what their child believes online.

Fair point first: knowing how a trick works is not the same as never falling for it. And the study below was run with adults, not children. Both of those matter.

Here is what it did. Researchers made five short videos. Each one explained a single trick used to mislead people online, before anyone met it for real: emotional words built to wind you up, arguments that contradict themselves, being offered only two choices when there are more, pinning the blame on one person or group, and attacking the person and not the point.

Across six controlled studies with 6,464 adults in the United States, those who watched one were better at recognising the trick straight afterwards than those who watched an unrelated video.

The honest reading: it measured spotting the trick, in adults, straight after watching. It did not follow anyone for months and it did not test children. So we would call it promising, not proven.

It is still the bit we find hopeful. A trick is easier to see once somebody has named it for you.

Tonight: pick one advert, there are plenty about this week, and ask "What is this one trying to make you feel? Why might someone want that?"

What was the first thing online that you remember being fooled by?

What stage is your child? Three questions, no sign up, link in bio.

post.first_comment: Source: Roozenbeek, van der Linden, Goldberg, Rathje and Lewandowsky, Psychological inoculation improves resilience against misinformation on social media, Science Advances, 2022. Six controlled studies with 6,464 adults in the United States, plus a field test on YouTube. It measured whether people could recognise a manipulation technique straight after watching a short video. It did not test children and it did not measure long term behaviour.
